rounds.riddle: July 1943: a crippled tanker sat dead in the water, broadside on, and a dozen of the boat's torpedoes struck her squarely, each a loud metallic clank, yet she would not sink. The torpedoman swore he had already disabled the magnetic trigger and set every fish to run shallow. So the captain swung the boat around to a sloppy, slanting angle that he would have scolded a cadet for. The slanted shot exploded; none of the perfect ones had.
rounds.chars: Lieutenant Commander Dan Daspit; Chief Hal Brenner (submarine torpedoman)
rounds.story: Daspit's Mark 14 torpedoes were duds even on contact settings, which Brenner had chosen precisely to rule out the famous problems of deep running and the faulty magnetic exploder. A lesser-known defect remained: the contact exploder's firing pin was so light that the violent deceleration of a dead-square 90° hit bent its guide rails before it could strike the cap, while a glancing oblique hit slowed the torpedo less and let the pin fire, so Daspit deliberately gave up the textbook beam shot for a sloppy angle.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Lt. Cmdr. Lawrence "Dan" Daspit, captain of the submarine USS *Tinosa*

**Character 2:** Chief Torpedoman's Mate (occupation: torpedoman), who had switched off the faulty magnetic feature on every Mark 14 torpedo so each would rely only on its contact exploder.

**Story:** Each perfect 90-degree hit on the Japanese tanker *Tonan Maru No. 3* stopped the torpedo so violently that the firing pin's guide bent and jammed before the pin could strike the detonator, so the warheads just clanged off her hull. Only when Daspit fired a sloppy glancing shot did the torpedo slow gently enough for the pin to fire and explode, exposing a flaw that the Navy later fixed with a lighter, stronger firing pin.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A accounts for both of the torpedoman's precautions, disabling the magnetic trigger and setting the torpedoes to run shallow, while Story B never explains the shallow setting.
rounds.fact:
REAL: The Mark 14 contact exploder had a real defect in which a perpendicular (90°) hit caused the firing pin to bind due to violent deceleration, so glancing hits of about 90° were less reliable, and Lt. Cdr. Dan Daspit's USS Tinosa test at Wahoo-era Pearl Harbor (July 1943) with the Tang Maru-like target and Chief Hal Brenner's involvement is documented.

Correction on details: Daspit's Tinosa fired at the Tama Maru on July 24, 1943, and every hit was a dud, which led to the famous test firing of a torpedo warhead into a cliff at Kahoolawe. That test confirmed the firing pin failure on perfect 90° impacts, and the fix was a lighter-weight pin design with better guidance. Brenner was indeed the torpedoman involved in the investigation. Daspit's choice of contact settings to rule out the magnetic exploder and depth problems is also accurate. The claim that he deliberately switched to a sloppy angle is a slight embellishment, since the oblique-angle remedy was more a lesson learned afterward, but the central mechanism is real.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
It explains why square hits jammed the contact exploder while the slanted hit worked, without A’s mistaken claim that the firing pin was too light.

rounds.riddle:
In Icelandic waters, with his trawler’s holds crammed with prime cod, Arnar made one final drag through the nursery shallows.
Instead of hiding the worthless runts, he insisted Sigurður log every single one on his measuring board.
When coastal radio broadcast an immediate fourteen-day ban across the entire grid, Arnar grinned.
He throttled toward harbor, leaving six frustrated rival boats hauling up their gear.
rounds.story: Arnar intentionally dragged the nursery so Sigurður would document that juvenile cod exceeded the legal catch threshold. Under Icelandic fisheries law, this triggered a mandatory, penalty-free *skyndilokun* (real-time closure) across the grid for fourteen days—the exact duration Arnar needed to steam to Reykjavík, offload his catch, and return before rivals could harvest the remaining mature stock.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Arnar, a trawler skipper whose holds are already full.

**Character 2 (with occupation):** Sigurður, a fisheries inspector from the Directorate of Fisheries, stationed on board to measure catches.

**Story:** Under Iceland's real-time closure rules, an area is automatically shut for fourteen days once an inspector records too many undersized juvenile cod, so Arnar, already loaded, deliberately trawled the nursery shallows and made sure Sigurður logged every runt. The juvenile count tripped the legal threshold and closed the grid to everyone, so Arnar steamed home with the only full catch while his six rivals had to haul up their gear empty-handed.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail without stretches: Arnar's full holds make the closure cost him nothing while it shuts out his rivals. Story B adds an implausible claim that he needs exactly fourteen days to offload and return.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Iceland does have *skyndilokun* (temporary real-time closures) triggered when inspectors find too many juveniles, but these are typically set by the Marine and Freshwater Research Institute and last about two weeks at most, and they close the area to all vessels. The riddle's premise that a fisherman could exploit this as a penalty-free tactic to reserve the remaining mature stock for himself, with the closure timed to his trip, is not how it works, since the closure would bar him as well and the "fourteen days" is not a fixed duration.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
Arnar’s full holds explain why he deliberately had every juvenile logged to trigger the immediate fourteen-day closure and force his six rivals to stop fishing, without assuming a precisely timed round trip.

rounds.riddle:
Permian Basin, night shift: the derrickman complained about rotten eggs for an hour, then grinned over the radio, "Smell's finally gone."
The man in the trailer glanced at the windsock, which had not moved, and turned pale.
He grabbed two air packs instead of one and ran toward the rig, not away from it.
He found the derrickman "asleep" on the rig floor and dragged him uphill, against the breeze.
rounds.chars: Dale Hutto; Ray Ortiz (drilling company man)
rounds.story: Ray knew the rotten-egg stink was hydrogen sulfide from a sour-gas pocket the bit had just cut into, and the motionless windsock told him the gas had not blown away. He also knew the lesser-known property of H2S: above roughly 100 ppm it paralyzes the sense of smell, so the smell "going away" meant the concentration was climbing toward a knockdown level. Following standard H2S rescue procedure, he put on one self-contained air pack and carried the second for Dale, who was already unconscious. He then hauled Dale upwind and uphill, because the gas is heavier than air and pools in low ground.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Rusty, the derrickman.
**Character 2:** Dale, the drilling rig's safety supervisor (H2S safety officer) in the trailer.

**Story:** Dale knew the windsock hadn't moved, so the gas hadn't blown away; Rusty's "smell's gone" meant hydrogen sulfide had risen high enough to deaden his sense of smell, the step just before collapse. Dale strapped on one air pack and carried a second for Rusty, then dragged his unconscious friend uphill and upwind, because heavy H2S pools in low ground and drifts downwind.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B covers every detail more completely: it names the sour-gas source, explains olfactory paralysis above about 100 ppm, and ties the second air pack and the uphill, upwind rescue to standard H2S procedure.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Hydrogen sulfide smells like rotten eggs at low levels but causes olfactory fatigue and paralysis of smell at roughly 100+ ppm, is heavier than air and pools in low areas, and standard rescue procedure calls for donning SCBA and moving victims upwind/uphill (or crosswind to higher ground).
rounds.alt_judge:
A
A explains the vanished smell, the two air packs, and the uphill, upwind rescue without inventing a newly struck sour-gas pocket.

rounds.riddle:
July 1943: a submarine crippled a giant tanker with two hasty, badly angled shots.
Then, from a perfect broadside position, it fired eleven careful torpedoes into the helpless ship, and the tanker stayed afloat.
With one torpedo left and the target dead in the water, the crew carried it home untouched.
Weeks later they cheered when a live warhead was dropped nose-first onto a steel plate and nothing happened.
rounds.chars: Lt. Cdr. Dan Daspit of USS Tinosa; his torpedoman's mate (torpedoman who maintained the Mark 14 torpedoes)
rounds.story: Daspit and his torpedoman realized that all eleven perfect shots had hit the tanker and failed to explode, so they saved the twelfth torpedo as untampered evidence that the weapon, not the crew, was at fault. The mechanism was the Mark 6 contact exploder: in a square 90-degree hit the sudden deceleration jammed the firing pin in its guides before it could strike the primer, while a glancing hit slowed the torpedo gently enough to fire, which is why only the two "bad" shots worked and why the crew cheered when the Pearl Harbor drop test onto steel produced a dud.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Lt. Cmdr. Lew Daspit, captain of the submarine USS *Tinosa*.

**Character 2:** Rear Adm. Charles "Swede" Momsen, a submarine force commander who ran the torpedo tests at Pearl Harbor.

**Story:** Daspit's two hasty, badly angled shots exploded, but the eleven perfect 90-degree hits on the tanker *Tonan Maru No. 3* were all duds, so he carried his last Mark 14 torpedo home as evidence. Momsen's team dropped live warheads nose-first onto steel plates, and the cheer came when one failed to explode, proving that a square hit crushed the firing pin before it could fire, which finally got the flawed exploder fixed.
rounds.judge:
B

Story B accounts for every detail: the two angled hits exploding, the eleven square hits failing, the last torpedo kept as evidence, and the cheer when Momsen's drop test proved the firing-pin flaw. It also gets the facts right, such as Daspit's name and the tanker's identity, where Story A slips.
rounds.fact:
REAL

The Mark 6 exploder problem on Mark 14 torpedoes was real: during the Tinosa/Tang Wahoo-era failures, Tinosa's July 1943 attack on the tanker Tonan Maru saw Daspit fire 11 torpedoes at it, and he saved the last one for analysis. The firing pin did bind under the sudden deceleration of a square hit (the Pearl Harbor test dropping a warhead onto steel produced a dud), whereas glancing hits let the pin function. The riddle's details are slightly embellished, such as the "only two bad shots worked" claim and the torpedoman's role, but the core mechanism is accurate.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
It better explains why the glancing hits worked, why the square hits and the drop test failed, and why the crew saved the last torpedo as untampered evidence.

rounds.riddle: At a Ryogoku sumo stable in 2019, a boy from Ulaanbaatar had swept floors for two years, waiting for the champion upstairs to receive his Japanese passport. The day it arrived, the old man who ran the house congratulated the champion, then bought the boy a ticket home.
rounds.chars: Temuulen, a 17-year-old Mongolian hopeful; Kiyonoyama (stablemaster, a retired wrestler who runs the stable)
rounds.story: Each stable is allowed only one foreign wrestler and the Mongolian champion held that slot, so Temuulen believed the champion's naturalization would free it for him. But since the Japan Sumo Association's 2010 revision the quota counts "foreign-born" wrestlers, so a passport frees nothing; the champion wanted citizenship only because it is required to own elder stock and inherit the stable, and when he announced on passport day that he would keep fighting rather than retire, Kiyonoyama knew the slot would stay filled for years and sent the boy home.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Batbold, a teenage Mongolian apprentice hoping to become a sumo wrestler.

**Character 2:** Oyakata Tanaka, the elderly stablemaster (retired wrestler) who runs the sumo stable.

**Story:** The Sumo Association allows each stable only one foreign-born wrestler, so Batbold swept floors for two years, hoping the champion's naturalization would open that single slot for him. When the passport arrived, Tanaka sadly explained that the rule counts wrestlers by birthplace, not passport, so the champion would hold the foreign slot until retirement, and then as a new Japanese citizen he could stay on as an elder and coach, leaving no place for Batbold and sending him home.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains the passport-day timing cleanly: the champion announces he will keep wrestling, so the foreign-born slot stays filled. Story B wrongly implies that the champion staying on as an elder would keep blocking a wrestler slot.
rounds.fact:
REAL

The Japan Sumo Association limits each stable to one foreign-born wrestler (the rule was revised in 2010 to count foreign-born wrestlers rather than foreign nationals, so naturalization does not free the slot), and Japanese citizenship is required to acquire elder stock (toshiyori) and run a stable, as seen with Hakuho and Asashoryu-era cases.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
Both stories explain why the passport didn’t free the slot, but A also explains why the stablemaster sent the boy home that day: the champion announced he would keep competing.

rounds.riddle:
Paris, 2023: while her whole night crew was on strike, Madame Vasseur's shop in the 11th never ran out of fresh bread.
Yet her ovens stayed cold all week, and a white van stopped at the back door at 5 a.m.
On the first morning she climbed a ladder and taped paper over a single word on her own awning.
Karim, picketing outside with his phone raised, lowered it in disappointment.
rounds.story: Since French labour law forbids hiring temps or fixed-term staff to replace strikers, Madame Vasseur kept her shelves full with loaves baked in a friend's shop across town and delivered by van before dawn. Karim, her striking baker, was waiting to photograph the storefront for the fraud inspectors, because the 1998 law reserves the word "Boulangerie" on a sign for shops where the dough is kneaded, shaped and baked on the premises, so by papering over that one word she could legally sell the outside bread and left him nothing to report.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Madame Vasseur, shop owner.
**Character 2:** Karim, a striking night-shift baker on her crew.

**Story:** French law lets a shop call itself a "Boulangerie" only if it kneads and bakes its own bread on site, so while her bakers struck, Madame Vasseur bought bread from an industrial supplier's 5 a.m. van and taped over "Boulangerie" on her awning, legally becoming a mere bread shop. Karim, who had been waiting to film the fraud and report her, saw the covered word, realized she was breaking no law, and lowered his phone.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail, including why the ovens stayed cold: French law bars hiring replacements for strikers, so outside bread was her only option, and papering over "Boulangerie" left Karim nothing to report.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The appellation "boulangerie" is genuinely protected in France (a 1998 law, codified in the Code de la consommation/Code rural), and French labour law does bar using CDD or temp workers to replace strikers (Code du travail L1242-6). But the claimed mechanism does not work as described: covering the word "Boulangerie" on the sign does not legally let a shop sell outside-baked bread, since the shop would still not be a boulangerie, and the "fraud inspectors" scheme and the temp-replacement link are contrived, though selling bread under another label (e.g., "dépôt de pain") is legal in a loose sense.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
It explains why she sourced bread from another bakery rather than hiring temporary replacements, and why covering “Boulangerie” left Karim with no misleading sign to photograph.

rounds.riddle: At 3 a.m. on a West Texas rig, the driller shouted "Kick!" and ten men ran toward the lights, not away. The only man who walked, calmly, went to the water tank and drank. By sunrise he'd been paid in full and sent home, and the well was never drilled deeper.
rounds.chars: Earl, a roughneck who was secretly a landman's spy; Dolores Vance (mudlogger, the geologist who sits in the logging trailer)
rounds.story: Earl was a lease-holder's cousin sent to watch the rig because the lease was about to expire. Under the lease's "habendum clause," a lease continues past its primary term only while the well is producing or actively drilling, and it has a lesser-known twist: once a well is completed as a dry hole, the lessee gets a short grace period (often 60–90 days) to begin new operations, otherwise everything reverts to the landowner. Dolores, the mudlogger, saw gas in the mud at 3 a.m., which is the "kick" that sent the crew rushing to the blowout preventer. Earl walked to the water tank calmly because he knew the kick was a small show of gas, not a gusher: he had salted the mud with a gas-releasing chemical to fake it, hoping to make the operator believe the formation was dangerous and plug the well. Once the operator officially plugged and abandoned the well as a dry hole at sunrise, the lease's grace-period clock started, and the crew was paid off and sent home without drilling deeper, so the landowner's family could reclaim the mineral rights when the clock ran out unused.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Hank, the night driller.

**Character 2:** Earl, a contract mud logger hired only to call the depth of the gas pay zone, paid in full once it was reached.

**Story:** When Hank yelled "Kick!", the crew sprinted to the lit BOP controls to shut in the well. Earl strolled to the water tank for a drink, because the gas surge meant they'd hit the reservoir exactly at the depth he'd predicted, so his job was done, the company sent him home paid by sunrise, and the well was completed right there instead of drilled deeper.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail simply: the kick shows that Earl's predicted pay zone was reached, so his job is finished, he is paid and sent home, and the well is completed at that depth. Story B needs convoluted lease clauses and sabotage, and it has the whole crew paid off rather than the one calm man.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The habendum clause and cessation-of-production/dry-hole provisions are real, but the scheme is not: those clauses typically let the lessee keep the lease by beginning new operations within a set period, so a dry hole starts a window for the lessee rather than a path to reversion. Faking a gas kick to force plugging, and a "grace-period clock" that returns the minerals to the landowner's family, do not work as described.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
A explains the crew’s rush to the lit well controls, Earl’s calm walk and prompt payoff, and the decision to stop drilling through a single event: reaching the target reservoir.

rounds.riddle: Paris, the week the boulangers walked out, the shelves on Rue Oberkampf stood bare. At dawn a man in a stained apron still carried warm loaves up the stairs of a building, but he knocked on only one door, and he took no money. The woman inside never opened it, and the loaves were left on the mat in a cloth bag stamped with a number.
rounds.chars: Madame Colette Vidal, an elderly widow who was once a union baker; Étienne Roux (a striking baker's journeyman, the occupation being baker)
rounds.story: Madame Vidal had been the strike committee's treasurer, and Étienne secretly baked for her because she was hiding the union's strike-fund ledger in her flat, and the loaves in the numbered bag were his coded way of reporting each day's count of striking members. He baked at all, and at dawn, because French law (the 1920s-era rule on night work in bakeries, which bans work in the small hours but allows a baker to make bread for his own household) let him treat Madame Vidal, whom he had legally registered as a dependent boarder, as family, and the lesser-known part is that this household exemption only permits unpaid bread, which is why he took no money and why the strikers could not call it scabbing.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Madame Rousseau, an elderly agoraphobic widow who hasn't opened her door in years.

**Character 2:** Luc, a striking boulanger who was once apprenticed to her late husband.

**Story:** Luc walked out with the other bakers but secretly fired up his old master's oven each dawn. He left free loaves for Madame Rousseau, who never opens her door to anyone, in her husband's old numbered delivery bag so she would know who had sent them.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail simply: a strike-breaking act of private loyalty, an agoraphobic widow who never opens her door, and the husband's numbered delivery bag as a signature. Story B depends on a convoluted coded ledger scheme and a dubious legal exemption.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The 1919 French law banning bakery night work (22 March 1919) was real, but it contains no household exemption letting a baker bake at dawn for a registered "dependent boarder" as family, nor any rule limiting such bread to unpaid production that would shield it from scabbing accusations.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
Luc’s loyalty to his late mentor naturally explains why he brings free bread to one door, why the widow leaves it closed, and why he uses her husband’s numbered bag.

rounds.riddle:
Off the Westfjords the trawler hauled its fattest cod of the season, and the deckhands swore at the sight of it.
The skipper had one tub in every twenty iced and tagged apart from the rest.
At the Ísafjörður auction those tagged fish fetched the best price of the week.
Yet when the share slips came, the men's cut from them was almost nothing.
rounds.chars: Gunnar, a deckhand on a share contract; Sigrún (trawler skipper)
rounds.story: The trawler had already used up its cod quota, so Sigrún could not land the big haul as ordinary catch, and the crew knew at once that a full net was mostly a headache for them. She kept the fish only by using Iceland's VS-afli rule, which lets a vessel land up to 5% of its catch outside quota (hence one tub in twenty tagged separately) if it is sold at public auction, with 80% of the proceeds paid to the state fisheries fund (Verkefnasjóður sjávarútvegsins), so Gunnar's share was calculated on only the boat's 20% despite the record price.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Jón, the deckhands' share-slip reader.
**Character 2:** Gunnar, the trawler skipper (occupation: fishing captain).

**Story:** The huge haul ran over the boat's cod quota, which made the deckhands curse, so Gunnar set aside one tub in twenty (5%) to land as "VS-catch." This is the Icelandic rule that lets a boat land up to 5% of its catch outside quota, provided it is sold at auction. The prime fish topped the Ísafjörður market, but by law about 80% of that money went straight to the state fisheries fund, leaving Jón and the crew almost nothing on their share slips.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B has the haul only running over quota, so the rest is landed as normal catch while the 5% goes out as VS-catch; Story A's "quota already used up" leaves the other nineteen tubs of the riddle unexplained.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Iceland does have a VS-afli ("viðbótarafli"/"VS" catch) rule under which a limited share of catch (about 5%) landed beyond quota is sold at auction, with the vessel keeping only about 20% of proceeds and the rest (80%) going to the Verkefnasjóður sjávarútvegsins, so the mechanism is essentially accurate.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
It ties the crew’s reaction to the already exhausted quota and explains why their shares were calculated on only the 20% the boat kept, despite the tagged fish fetching the week’s best price.

rounds.riddle: Reykjavík, 1976: the trawler turned for home with her hold half empty, the skipper refusing to radio why. A man in a clean suit waited on the quay, and he boarded before the lines were fast. He left with only the logbook, and the crew were paid in full that week.
rounds.chars: Gunnar, a trawler skipper; Halldór, a Coast Guard legal officer (Landhelgisgæslan)
rounds.story: During the Third Cod War, Gunnar's trawler had been caught inside the disputed 200-mile zone by a British frigate and had its net cut, and he turned for home knowing the catch was ruined. Halldór boarded at once to seize the logbook, because under Icelandic fisheries rules a vessel's log is the legal evidence for compensation claims, and the lesser-known part is that the state insurance fund pays crews' guaranteed wages for a cut-net incident only if the log is certified by an official before the vessel is moored, which explains why he boarded before the lines were fast and why the crew was paid that very week.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The trawler's skipper.

**Character 2:** An Icelandic Foreign Ministry lawyer (occupation: government diplomat preparing Iceland's case in the Cod War).

**Story:** During the 1976 Cod War, a British frigate rammed the trawler and cut her nets mid-trip, so the skipper turned home half-full and kept radio silence so the British wouldn't hear and dispute his account. The ministry lawyer rushed aboard to seize the logbook, with its exact positions inside Iceland's 200-mile limit, as evidence for the NATO negotiations, and the government quietly compensated the crew's lost catch in full.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A naturally explains the skipper's radio silence (keeping the British from hearing and disputing his account), the suited diplomat, and the logbook seized as evidence, while Story B leaves the radio refusal unexplained and rests on a contrived certification rule.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
Iceland did have a state compensation arrangement of sorts during the Cod Wars, but I know of no rule that a certified log must be official-verified before mooring for the insurance fund to pay guaranteed wages for cut-net incidents, and the Coast Guard legal officer seizing the log for that purpose appears fabricated.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
The pre-mooring certification rule directly links the man’s haste, his taking only the logbook, and the crew’s prompt full pay, though it leaves the skipper’s radio silence unexplained.

rounds.riddle:
Across 1974 Paris, iron grates stayed barred and flourless streets starved for a single crust.
Only Luc’s oven blazed on Monday dawn, drawing three hundred famished souls to his counter.
Yet Laurent pushed past the cheering crowd not to disperse them, but to order the fire extinguished.
Ignoring the thirty dark shops on the boulevard, he fined the sole provider and forced his shutters down.
rounds.story: During the 1974 Paris bakery strike, Luc defied the collective walkout to bake bread for the city's starving residents. However, Laurent was obligated to shut him down under the Paris prefectural decree enforcing mandatory weekly bakery closures, which granted no strike exemptions and made opening on Luc’s registered Monday rest day a punishable labor offense.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Luc, a baker
**Character 2:** Laurent, a labor inspector for the Paris prefecture

**Story:** Under a 1974 prefectoral decree, every bakery in Luc's district had to take the same mandatory weekly rest day, Monday, so the thirty dark shops were simply obeying the law. Luc fired his oven anyway to capture all their customers, so Laurent ignored the cheering crowd and fined the only rule-breaker on the boulevard, forcing his shutters down to protect the bakers who had played fair.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A explains everything with a single cause: a mandatory Monday rest day accounts for the thirty dark shops, the crowd at the one open oven, and the inspector fining only the rule-breaker, while Story B awkwardly layers a strike on top of the same decree.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
There was no 1974 Paris bakery strike of this kind, and while France did have prefectural decrees requiring weekly bakery closure days (staggered by arrondissement/department), the specific story of "Luc" and "Laurent" and a registered Monday rest day enforced against a strike-breaking baker appears fabricated.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
The strike explains the widespread hunger and cheering crowd, while Luc’s mandatory Monday closure explains why Laurent fined him alone despite the shortage.

rounds.riddle:
When Midland mud violently burped and the shuddering derrick groaned,
Travis screamed to throw the red switch and seal the well before they blew.
Yet Hoyt stalled, throttling the drawworks to haul the drillstring four feet higher,
Refusing to trip the shearing blades until a painted white ring cleared the floor.
rounds.story: A catastrophic high-pressure gas kick was erupting up the borehole, requiring the crew to activate the blowout preventer's emergency shear rams to sever the pipe and cap the well. Because blowout preventer blades can slice standard pipe body but will catastrophically jam against a thickened, alloy-hardened tool joint, Hoyt executed a mandatory well-control "space-out" by hoisting the string until the painted white tally mark proved the pipe collar was safely clear of the cutting blades.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Travis, a panicked young roughneck.

**Character 2:** Hoyt, a veteran driller (occupation: oil-rig driller).

**Story:** When the Midland well kicked, Travis begged Hoyt to slam the blowout preventer shut immediately. Hoyt knew a thick tool joint was sitting right in the shear rams, where the blades would jam instead of cutting, so he hauled the pipe up four feet until the painted white spacing mark showed the thin pipe body was in place, then sheared and sealed the well cleanly.
rounds.judge:
B
Both stories give the same tool-joint space-out explanation, but B states outright that a thick joint sat in the shear rams, ties the four-foot lift to the white mark, and ends with the well sheared and sealed cleanly.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Spacing out the drill string so a tool joint isn't aligned with the blind shear rams is standard well-control practice, since shear rams generally can't cut through tool joints (and often the pipe body is what's sheared), though the "painted white tally mark" is a plausible marker detail rather than a universal standard.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
It explicitly connects the four-foot lift and the white ring clearing the floor to moving the obstructing tool joint out of the shear rams and putting cuttable pipe in its place.

rounds.riddle:
In a Ryōgoku stable, the top wrestler swore allegiance to Japan, and the master poured sake for everyone.
The next morning a boy from Ulaanbaatar knocked, and the master shut the door on him.
"Come back the day after he steps out of the ring for the last time," the master said, nodding at the new citizen.
The top wrestler bowed to the boy and was not offended at all.
rounds.chars: Ganbaatar, a Mongolian-born wrestler; Master Takeda (sumo stablemaster)
rounds.story: Ganbaatar took Japanese citizenship because the Japan Sumo Association only lets Japanese nationals buy elder stock and later run a stable, so the sake was for his future as an oyakata. Since 2010, however, the Association's rule of one foreign wrestler per stable counts wrestlers by foreign birth rather than by passport, so the naturalized Ganbaatar still filled Takeda's only foreign slot, and that slot would open for the Mongolian boy only once Ganbaatar retired.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Batbayar, a Mongolian-born yokozuna who has just become a Japanese citizen.

**Character 2 (with occupation):** The stablemaster (oyakata) of a Ryōgoku sumo stable.

**Story:** The master poured sake because Batbayar's new citizenship meant he could one day become a sumo elder and inherit the stable. But under the Sumo Association's one-foreign-born-wrestler-per-stable rule, a naturalized wrestler still occupies the foreign slot, so Batbayar's young cousin from Ulaanbaatar must wait until the yokozuna retires, and Batbayar bowed to the boy understanding fully that the door had been shut by the rule, not the master.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail, including why the top wrestler bowed and took no offense (the boy is his cousin, and he knows the rule, not the master, shut the door), while Story B never addresses the bow.
rounds.fact:
REAL

The Japan Sumo Association does require Japanese citizenship to acquire elder stock (toshiyori kabu) and become an oyakata, and since 2002 its one-foreign-wrestler-per-stable rule has counted naturalized wrestlers as foreign-born, though the rule dates from 2002 rather than 2010 (2010 was when the limit was tightened to exclude naturalized wrestlers from being exempt), which counts as a minor embellishment.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
Both stories explain the celebration and the recruitment rule, but A also explains why the wrestler bowed without taking offense: he knew the master was enforcing the rule.

rounds.riddle:
Three days after the Tokyo tournament ended, with the new rankings sealed for another month, the old man with the combs bowed low to the boy whose hair he had yanked for six years.
He had shaped that hair into the ginkgo-leaf fan exactly once, for a single afternoon mid-tournament; now he promised it for every fighting day.
By evening the boy who scrubbed his seniors' backs had a back-scrubber of his own, and an embroiderer was at the stable door with a tape measure.
No one in the stable had peeked at the secret list.
rounds.chars: Daiki, a makushita-division wrestler at a Ryogoku stable; Tokomasa (tokoyama, the stable's sumo hairdresser)
rounds.story: Daiki had just been promoted to juryo and so became a sekitori, a rank that brings the ginkgo-leaf oicho topknot, personal attendants and a deep bow from the hairdresser who used to boss him around. Nobody needed to peek, because the Sumo Association officially announces juryo promotions alone at its ranking meeting on the Wednesday after a tournament, while the rest of the banzuke stays secret for weeks, precisely so that new sekitori can order their embroidered kesho-mawashi in time, which is why the embroiderer came that same day; and Tokomasa had tied the fan once before because a makushita wrestler scheduled against a juryo opponent must wear the oicho for that one bout.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kenta, a young makushita-ranked sumo wrestler.

**Character 2:** Old Mr. Sato, the stable's *tokoyama* (sumo hairdresser).

**Story:** Kenta had worn the ginkgo-leaf *ōichō-mage* topknot only once, on the afternoon mid-tournament when he was matched up against a jūryō wrestler. Three days after the Tokyo basho, the Sumo Association announced his promotion to jūryō, ahead of the still-secret banzuke ranking list. That made him a salaried sekitori, so Sato bowed and promised him the topknot for every bout, a junior was assigned to scrub his back, and an embroiderer came to measure him for his ceremonial apron.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains more of the odd details: why juryo promotions alone are announced early while the banzuke stays sealed (so new sekitori can order their kesho-mawashi in time), why the embroiderer arrived that same day, and why the hairdresser's bow reverses six years of hierarchy.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The Sumo Association does announce new juryo promotions shortly after the banzuke-compiling meeting (before the full banzuke is published), and sekitori get the oicho and kesho-mawashi, but the claim that a makushita wrestler facing a juryo opponent must wear the oicho for that bout is false, since makushita wrestlers wear the chonmage and only sekitori wear the oicho, apart from the special case of a top-ranked makushita wrestler fighting in a juryo bout, which does not require it by rule.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
It better explains the one-off topknot and why the embroiderer arrived that day: jūryō promotions are announced early so new sekitori can order ceremonial aprons while the full rankings remain secret.

rounds.riddle:
At a Speyside distillery, a cask filled the day Fiona was born was to be opened on her 50th birthday.
Eleven months before the party, Callum floated a small glass instrument in a sample and read one number.
The cask was emptied into bottles that same week, each labelled "49".
Fiona thanked him for ruining her plan.
rounds.chars: Fiona, the cask's owner; Callum (distillery warehouse manager)
rounds.story: Callum's hydrometer showed that Fiona's birth cask had slipped to 40.3% alcohol, because in a damp Scottish warehouse a cask loses strength as well as volume every year. Under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 anything bottled below 40% cannot legally be sold as Scotch whisky, and age counts only completed years in oak, so he bottled it at once as a 49-year-old rather than let eleven more months turn her fortune into a nameless "spirit drink".
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Fiona, the woman whose birth-year cask was being saved for her 50th birthday.

**Character 2:** Callum, the distillery's master blender.

**Story:** Callum's hydrometer showed that decades of "angel's share" evaporation had pulled the cask's strength down to just above 40% ABV, the legal minimum for Scotch whisky, so another eleven months would have left it unsellable as whisky. He bottled it that week as a 49-year-old, and Fiona, half rueful and half grateful, thanked him for ruining her perfect 50th-birthday plan while saving the whisky itself.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A explains every detail more completely: why a damp Scottish warehouse lowers the strength, the legal 40% threshold that made waiting impossible, and why the label had to read "49" (only completed years in oak count), whereas B asserts the "49" label without explaining it.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 require a minimum bottling strength of 40% ABV, casks do lose alcohol strength in damp warehouses (the "angel's share" can lower ABV when humidity is high), and the age statement must reflect the youngest spirit's completed years in the cask.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
It connects the hydrometer reading and the “49” labels to Fiona’s gratitude: bottling early spoiled her birthday plan but saved the cask’s contents from falling below the legal minimum strength for Scotch whisky.

rounds.riddle:
At an Islay distillery, a cask filled in 1969 was measured on Monday; the owner went white and binned the "50 Years Old" labels.
The man with the hydrometer said, "Wait till Thursday," though the stronger cask he wanted stood ready beside him.
On Thursday he tipped a single pail from it into the old cask, and the owner smiled again.
The bottles went on sale with no age and no year printed on them at all.
rounds.chars: Morag, the distillery owner; Ewan (master blender)
rounds.story: Monday's reading showed that fifty years of evaporation had sunk the 1969 cask to 39.6% ABV, below the 40% legal minimum for bottling as Scotch whisky, so Ewan the master blender planned to lift it back over the line with a pail of cask-strength spirit at 63%. But that young cask only reached its third birthday on Thursday, and under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 spirit under three years in oak is not yet whisky and would have disqualified the whole cask, while once it was added any age statement had to give the youngest component (3 years) and a vintage year is allowed only if every drop was distilled in that year, so Morag printed neither.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The distillery owner.
**Character 2:** The warehouse manager, the man with the hydrometer.

**Story:** On Monday the hydrometer showed that the 1969 cask had lost so much strength to the angels' share that it had fallen below 40% ABV, the legal minimum for Scotch whisky, so it could not be sold as whisky at all, let alone as "50 Years Old." The manager's stronger cask had been filled exactly three years earlier on a Thursday, so he waited until it legally became whisky, then tipped in one pail to lift the old cask above 40%. Because the law says an age statement must give the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle, the honest label would have read "3 Years Old," so they sold it with no age or year printed at all.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A explains both missing details: the age statement would have to read "3 years" because of the young spirit, and a vintage year is banned once spirit from another year is blended in, while Story B never justifies leaving off the year.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, Scotch must be matured in oak for at least three years and bottled at a minimum of 40% ABV. An age statement must refer to the youngest component, and a vintage claim requires that all of the spirit was distilled in that year, so the mechanism is described accurately.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
Both stories explain the low strength, the wait until Thursday, and the discarded age labels, but A also explains why the blend could no longer carry the 1969 vintage.

rounds.riddle:
At a Speyside distillery, the blender tipped a single thimble of last spring's clear spirit into the 30-year-old vat.
The valuer came next morning and wrote down a tenth of yesterday's figure.
The laird, mid-divorce, poured her a dram in thanks.
It tasted exactly the same.
rounds.chars: Laird Callum Grant, the distillery owner; Morag Reid (master blender)
rounds.story: Callum was in the middle of a divorce, and his wife's lawyers were about to have the distillery's prized 30-year-old stock valued as matrimonial assets, so he quietly asked Morag to make that stock worth far less on paper before the valuer arrived. She tipped in one thimble of spirit distilled only the previous spring, because under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 spirit must mature in oak in Scotland for at least three years to be called Scotch whisky, and any age statement must reflect the youngest spirit in the mix; that single thimble legally turned the whole vat into unnamed sub-three-year spirit, which crashed its valuation overnight while its taste stayed exactly the same.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The Laird, a distillery owner in the middle of a bitter divorce.

**Character 2:** Morag, the distillery's master blender.

**Story:** Because Scotch law sets a blend's age by its youngest drop, Morag's single thimble of months-old new-make spirit legally turned the laird's priceless 30-year-old vat into young spirit that can't even be called whisky. The valuer had to mark it at a tenth of its worth, shrinking the asset his wife would claim in the settlement, so the laird poured Morag a grateful dram, and of course it tasted exactly the same.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A covers every detail more completely: the laird's request explains the thanks, and the three-year maturation rule plus the youngest-spirit age rule explains the crash to a tenth while the taste stays the same.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The age-statement rule is real (the age on the label must reflect the youngest whisky in the blend), but adding a young spirit would not turn the whole vat into "sub-three-year spirit" that is legally unnamed. The vat would simply have to carry a age statement of the youngest component, or none, and the blend would lose its Scotch status only if the young component itself failed the three-year requirement, so the "crashing" mechanism is materially wrong. Also, a 30-year-old stock's value as an asset would not legally be erased by this, since the valuer would assess the actual contents.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
It explains how the thimble could strip the vat of its Scotch whisky status and slash its divorce valuation without noticeably changing the taste, and identifies the blender as the person thanked.

rounds.riddle:
Off Iceland's Westfjords, skipper Gunnar's trawler hauled cod so small that a stranger aboard laid each on a board and wrote down numbers.
Gunnar threw none back, though they would fetch almost nothing at auction.
He had them iced in tubs apart from the rest and kept counting small tubs against full ones.
The moment the small tubs reached one in ten, he left the richest ground of the trip.
rounds.chars: Gunnar, the trawler's skipper; Sigrún (a Fiskistofa fisheries inspector riding along as on-board observer)
rounds.story: Sigrún was a Directorate of Fisheries inspector measuring the catch, and with her watching Gunnar could not break Iceland's discard ban, so every worthless undersized cod had to be kept and landed against his quota. He stowed them apart because the regulations count cod under 50 cm at only half weight against quota if kept separate, but only up to 10% of the trip's cod catch, so once his small tubs hit one in ten every further small fish would cost full quota and he steamed off.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Gunnar, a trawler skipper.

**Character 2:** Sigrún, a fisheries inspector from Iceland's Directorate of Fisheries, riding along to measure catch lengths.

**Story:** Iceland bans throwing fish back, so Gunnar had to land every undersized cod Sigrún measured, keeping them iced apart because juveniles up to a set share of the catch count only lightly against his quota. When the small tubs hit one in ten, he knew Sigrún's numbers would trigger a quick closure of the ground to protect the young cod, and past that share every small fish would eat his full quota, so he left the rich ground before either happened.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail with one coherent rule: the discard ban enforced by the observer, small cod counted at half weight only up to 10% of the catch. Story B muddles this by adding a speculative ground-closure trigger and leaves the quota rule vague.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Iceland does have a discard ban and Fiskistofa inspectors, and undersized fish can be landed as "VS-afli" (not counted against quota, with a limit of about 5% of catch), but the specific rule of cod under 50 cm counting at half weight up to 10% does not match the real mechanism.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
The discard ban explains why Gunnar kept the small cod, and the separate storage and departure at one in ten follow from the quota discount without assuming an imminent closure.

rounds.riddle:
In a Tokyo stable before dawn, the youngest boy hid the old man's scissors and was thanked for it.
The man wept when his topknot stayed put, yet he had come in the full dress he wears only for ceremonies.
Every wrestler bowed to him, and none of them dared to ask when he'd be done.
At noon the boy's belt was retied by someone who had never wrestled.
rounds.chars: Takeshi, a 15-year-old new recruit who has just joined the stable; Master Oyama, a retired yokozuna's hairdresser (tokoyama) attending a retirement ceremony
rounds.story: The old stable master, a former wrestler, was holding his danpatsu-shiki (retirement haircut ceremony), where guests each snip one lock of his topknot and the tokoyama cuts the final strand, so the boy hid the tokoyama's scissors, which delayed the cutting and let the master keep his topknot a little longer, and the master wept with gratitude. The real-world mechanism is the Japan Sumo Association's rule that a retiring wrestler's ceremony must occur in the Ryōgoku Kokugikan with a hairdresser who must be a certified tokoyama, so no substitute could be used and nobody dared ask for the end; since the tokoyama also ties the sagari and the mawashi for sekitori-rank wrestlers, the boy, not yet ranked, was retied at noon by the tokoyama as a courtesy after the scissors were found, and only a tokoyama, who never wrestled, could do it.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kenta, the stable's youngest apprentice.

**Character 2:** Takanoyama, an aging sekitori (sumo wrestler) who came in formal montsuki dress for his own topknot-cutting retirement ceremony.

**Story:** Before dawn, Kenta hid the ceremonial scissors, and Takanoyama wept with relief, because the stablemaster had pressured him to retire after an injury he secretly felt healed from. He thanked the boy and announced he would keep wrestling, so every wrestler bowed in respect and none dared ask when he'd be done; at noon the stablemaster's wife, who had never wrestled, retied Kenta's loosened mawashi with pride.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A coherently explains every detail: the hidden scissors save the topknot, the man wept and gave thanks, the ceremonial dress, and the reverent wrestlers, whereas Story B relies on invented rules and contradicts the stable setting by moving the ceremony to the Kokugikan.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The danpatsu-shiki is real and guests do snip the topknot with the tokoyama cutting last, but the claimed rule that a certified tokoyama is required and no substitute is allowed is not an actual Sumo Association regulation. Tokoyama also don't tie the sagari or mawashi, since wrestlers' attendants (tsukebito) and the wrestlers themselves handle those, so the account is materially wrong.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
A directly explains the ceremonial dress, tears, gratitude, and respectful silence, while B splits the old man’s role between two people and invokes a venue rule that clashes with the stable setting.

rounds.riddle:
When the commander sounded the dive klaxon in 1943, the deck plunged steeply toward the deep.
Without an explosion or hull breach, every man collapsed, blood leaking from their ears.
An arctic, blinding white fog swallowed the bone-dry compartment in a single second.
Ignoring the sudden winter, the veteran bypassed the life preservers and threw all his weight onto a fuel lever.
rounds.chars: Commander Vance; Chief Henderson (motor machinist's mate)
rounds.story: When Commander Vance ordered an emergency crash dive, the bridge crew shut the main induction valve before Chief Henderson could disengage the diesels, allowing the running engines to violently suck the atmosphere out of the sealed hull. Standard naval dive procedure mandated tripping the diesel fuel racks prior to closing the airway, as the running cylinders otherwise acted as massive vacuum pumps, causing a catastrophic depressurization that ruptured the crew's eardrums outward and induced severe adiabatic cooling, flash-condensing the humid air into freezing white fog.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The young U-boat commander

**Character 2:** The veteran chief engine-room mechanic (submarine machinist)

**Story:** When the commander ordered a crash dive, the main air-induction valve slammed shut, but the diesel engines kept running and sucked the air out of the sealed boat. The sudden vacuum burst the crew's eardrums and flash-chilled the humid air into freezing fog, so the veteran ignored the lifejackets (nothing was flooding) and yanked the fuel cut-off lever to starve the diesels before they suffocated everyone.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B explicitly explains every clue, including why the veteran ignored the lifejackets (nothing was flooding) and threw himself onto the fuel cut-off lever to stop the vacuum, while Story A never actually describes the final action.
rounds.fact:
REAL

This is a documented hazard on WWII-era diesel submarines: if the main induction was shut while the engines were still drawing air, they could pull a significant vacuum in the boat, which caused ear pain and injuries and fog from rapid cooling. The details are embellished, since the usual procedure was to stop the engines or shift to the "bottled" air arrangement, but the basic mechanism is accurate.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
Both stories explain the bleeding ears and sudden fog, but B also explains why the veteran ignored the life preservers and grabbed the fuel lever: the boat wasn’t flooding, and cutting the fuel would stop the diesels from drawing down the cabin air.

rounds.riddle:
Through a snowy Tokyo dawn, a scarred heavyweight trudges barefoot in wooden clogs, his toes turning blue.
Ahead strides a teenager in warm split-toe socks, whose travel bags the veteran obediently carries.
Just yesterday, the youth knelt at his feet to scrub his back and ladle his morning broth.
But a parchment delivered at six stripped the elder's bleached white sash and handed him black.
rounds.story: When the Japan Sumo Association's official banzuke ranking was delivered at six that morning, Daiki dropped from the salaried Juryo division to unsalaried Makushita while the teenage Ren was promoted, stripping Daiki of his white practice belt and forcing him to become Ren's attendant. Under the Association's strict Dress Code regulations, unsalaried wrestlers are legally prohibited from wearing tabi socks outdoors regardless of winter weather, leaving Daiki barefoot in wooden clogs while Ren earned the sekitori privilege of wearing them.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kenji, a scarred veteran sumo wrestler, just demoted from the salaried juryo division.

**Character 2:** Taro, a teenage sumo wrestler (rikishi) from the same stable, who was Kenji's tsukebito (personal attendant) until yesterday.

**Story:** When the new banzuke ranking sheet was posted at six, it dropped Kenji below sekitori rank, costing him his white practice mawashi, his warm tabi socks and his attendants. It also promoted Taro, so this snowy morning the veteran trudges barefoot in geta behind the boy he once ordered around, carrying the bags of the teen who used to scrub his back and serve his chanko.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A explains every detail naturally: the scars, the back-scrubbing and broth-serving, the white-to-black belt swap and the role reversal. Story B leaves out the attendant duties and overstates sumo custom as legally prohibited dress-code rules.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The banzuke promotion/demotion system between Juryo and Makushita is real, but the details are wrong: sekitori (Juryo and above) wear a white training mawashi while lower ranks wear black or dark cotton ones, and the footwear rules are different. Lower-ranked wrestlers (Makushita and below) are restricted to geta and cannot wear tabi or socks, yet the claim that this is "legally prohibited" under a Dress Code regulation with socks specifically is exaggerated, and the "six that morning" delivery and the forced-attendant story are embellished.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
It explains the reversal through the wrestlers’ change in rank, identifies the teen as the veteran’s former attendant, and accounts for the belt and socks without claiming that going sockless was a legal requirement.

rounds.riddle: In a Ryōgoku stable, Batbayar traded his Mongolian passport for a Japanese one, yet his teenage cousin still had to wait in Ulaanbaatar. The cousin's suitcase arrived only on the day Batbayar's topknot was cut off. Batbayar never left the stable; he simply began giving the orders there. Why did the cousin need the topknot gone and not the passport?
rounds.chars: Temuulen, Batbayar's teenage cousin; Batbayar (sumo wrestler)
rounds.story: Batbayar took Japanese citizenship because the Japan Sumo Association lets only Japanese nationals buy elder stock and stay on as coaches, but its one-foreigner-per-stable rule counts wrestlers by birthplace, so even after naturalizing he still filled the stable's single foreign slot and Temuulen could not be recruited. Only when Batbayar retired at his topknot-cutting ceremony and became an elder did he stop counting as an active foreign wrestler, which freed the slot, so his cousin moved in that same day as the stable's new foreign recruit under Batbayar's command.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Batbayar, a Mongolian-born sumo wrestler who retires and becomes a stablemaster (oyakata).
**Character 2:** His teenage cousin, an aspiring sumo apprentice waiting in Ulaanbaatar.

**Story:** The Sumo Association allows each stable only one foreign-born wrestler, and naturalization doesn't change that, so Batbayar's new Japanese passport still left him filling the stable's single "foreign" slot. Only when his topknot was cut at his retirement ceremony did that slot open, and Batbayar, now eligible to coach because he was a Japanese citizen, took over the stable and immediately sent for his cousin.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A explains the passport (needed to buy elder stock), the topknot (retirement frees the foreign slot), and the same-day suitcase (the cousin moved in that day), whereas B's "sent for his cousin" makes a same-day arrival less natural.
rounds.fact:
REAL

The Japan Sumo Association does require elders to be Japanese citizens (which is why foreign-born wrestlers like Hakuho and Kyokushuzan naturalized), and it limits each stable to one foreign-born wrestler, a rule that counts by birthplace so naturalized wrestlers still occupy the slot. The scenario is fictional, but the mechanism is accurate: a retired wrestler turned elder no longer counts as an active wrestler, which frees the slot.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
It directly explains why the cousin could move in that very day: Batbayar’s citizenship let him stay on as a coach, but only his retirement freed the stable’s foreign-born wrestler slot.

rounds.riddle: In Speyside, the stillhouse floor was swept at dawn, yet the cask sat unfilled for three years. The excise officer's brass-locked ledger recorded 40 gallons "lost" before a drop was ever poured. The distiller toasted him anyway, then paid more duty on a smaller barrel.
rounds.chars: Isla MacAllan, a widowed distiller's heir who inherited the stillhouse; Mr. Dunbar (excise officer)
rounds.story: Isla's late husband had secretly stored smuggled foreign-grain spirit in the empty-looking cask, and Dunbar, doing the gauge by dip-rod, discovered it was already full, so he entered the "lost" 40 gallons as evaporation to shield her from a seizure of the whole stillhouse. The real-world mechanism is that spirit in bond is taxed on its gauged volume at the time of filling, with the "angels' share" evaporation allowance only reducing duty for spirit legally entered into warehouse; so by the lesser-known rule, once Dunbar recorded the cask as filled retroactively at the three-year-old filling date, the duty was due on its original filled strength, and Isla paid more duty on a smaller barrel because the evaporation had already shrunk it while the tax was fixed on the larger entry volume.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Angus, the distiller.
**Character 2:** Mr. Reid, an excise officer (a Victorian "gauger" who measured casks for tax).

**Story:** Angus's great cask had sat empty in the swept stillhouse for three years, and its staves dried and shrank, so Mr. Reid re-gauged it and wrote 40 gallons of capacity as "lost" in his locked ledger before any spirit went in. Angus toasted the honest gauger for catching it, since filling the shrunken cask at its old rating would have looked like smuggling, and he gladly paid more duty on the smaller, tighter barrel because less of his whisky escaped as the angels' share.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A coherently explains the empty cask, the 40 gallons "lost" in capacity before any pour, the toast, and the higher duty on a tighter barrel. Story B contradicts the riddle by making the cask secretly full and relies on a convoluted, invented tax rule.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
Duty on bonded spirit is generally charged on the quantity actually removed from bond (with allowances for losses like evaporation), not fixed on the original fill volume, and the narrative's "retroactive entry" and duty-on-original-volume mechanism is internally muddled and not how bonded warehousing works.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
A takes the three years of emptiness literally and explains the recorded loss as reduced capacity, whereas B requires the supposedly unfilled cask to have been secretly full.

rounds.riddle: In 1943, a submarine lay silent on the bottom while the enemy's search above grew louder. The cook was told to stop baking and the captain ordered every man to lie still in his bunk. Yet one sailor was allowed to keep a candle burning, and an hour later the boat rose and escaped.
rounds.chars: Captain of a U.S. fleet submarine; Chemical-supply storekeeper (pharmacist's mate) who handled the boat's carbon dioxide absorbent (lithium hydroxide / soda lime)
rounds.story: During a long depth-charge hunt the boat ran out of fresh air, so the pharmacist's mate (fact 1: the air was becoming foul with CO2) kept a candle burning as a gauge, because a flame dies when oxygen falls to about 16% and so shows the air going bad. The men were ordered to lie still and the baking stopped to cut oxygen use, and the lesser-known mechanism (fact 2) is that CO2 absorbent such as soda lime works poorly when cold and releases heat as it reacts, so he spread the absorbent near the warm candle, and when the flame guttered the captain judged it time to surface in the dark after an hour, knowing the candle's flame would gutter from CO2 buildup well before the men would feel symptoms.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The Captain
**Character 2:** Seaman Hale, the boat's electrician's mate (occupation: electrician's mate)

**Story:** With the batteries nearly dead and the air running out, the Captain stopped the oven and made the men lie still so they would use as little oxygen as possible. He let Hale keep one candle lit as a gauge of the air: when its flame shrank and guttered an hour later, the Captain knew they could wait no longer, surfaced into the darkness the enemy had just left, and slipped away.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains each detail simply (oxygen conservation, the candle as an air gauge, surfacing once the enemy had left), while Story B adds a convoluted and dubious absorbent-warming mechanism and contradicts itself about whether the flame responds to oxygen or CO2.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The candle-as-gauge idea has some real basis, but the account is materially wrong: a flame goes out at roughly 16% oxygen, which is not a reliable early warning for CO2, so it would not gutter "well before symptoms" from CO2 buildup. The claim that spreading absorbent near a candle helps is also dubious, since soda lime does release heat as it reacts but it doesn't need an external flame, and lithium hydroxide is not used that way.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
It explains the stillness, the halted baking, and the candle as an effort to conserve and monitor the remaining air, without B’s strained claims about candle-warmed absorbent and early CO₂ warning.

rounds.riddle: In 1919 the Paris oven men walked out, and they won. The master paid no extra wage, yet he cursed the clock above his door. He used the same flour and the same oven, but his loaves came out thin as a cane. And not one was late for breakfast.
rounds.chars: Émile Roux; Gaston Lefèvre (master baker on the rue Mouffetard)
rounds.story: Émile and his fellow Paris bakery workers struck against the brutal all-night shifts, so their demand was about hours, not pay, and the master Gaston lost no money in wages. The French law of 28 March 1919 banned bakery work between 10 p.m. and 4 a.m., which left too little time for a fat round loaf to rise and bake before customers arrived. Gaston had to shape his dough into long, thin sticks, which rise and bake far faster, so his bread was still ready by breakfast.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Jacques, a Paris baker's journeyman (an oven man)
**Character 2:** Monsieur Duval, a master baker (occupation: boulanger)

**Story:** After the 1919 strike, the new law forbade Jacques and his fellow oven men from working between 10 p.m. and 4 a.m., so Monsieur Duval paid no extra wage but cursed the clock that now kept his ovens cold all night. With too few hours left to bake his fat round loaves, he shaped the same dough into long, thin baguettes that baked in a fraction of the time, and every one was out of the oven before breakfast.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B explains every detail, including why the master paid no extra wage (the strike was about hours, not pay), which Story A simply asserts without explanation.
rounds.fact:
REAL

The 1919 French decree banning bakery work from 10 p.m. to 4 a.m. is a widely cited explanation for the baguette's popularity, as thin loaves bake faster. The specific named individuals (Roux, Lefèvre) are likely fictional illustrations, but the legal mechanism is real, even though historians dispute how much it actually shaped the baguette's origin.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
It ties the clock to the new work hours and explains how thinner loaves baked in time for breakfast without assuming they also rose faster.

rounds.riddle:
At a camp above Iten, a stranger met Kiprop at the gate after his 40 km long run and would not let him out of sight, even in the toilet.
Kiprop, gulping water, handed over what the stranger wanted within twenty minutes.
Yet the stranger stayed four more hours, urged the thirsty man to stop drinking, and took the same thing twice more.
He was satisfied only by the third, but carried all three away.
rounds.chars: Kiprop, a marathon runner at an Iten training camp; Daniel (doping control officer)
rounds.story: Daniel was an anti-doping officer making an unannounced out-of-competition test, so once he had notified Kiprop he had to keep him under continuous observation and witness the urine leave his body. Because Kiprop had drunk litres after his run, his first two samples fell below the WADA minimum specific gravity of 1.005 on Daniel's refractometer, and the rules require the officer to keep collecting until a sample is concentrated enough, to advise against further drinking, and to send every sample, dilute ones included, to the laboratory.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kiprop, a Kenyan marathon runner.

**Character 2:** An anti-doping control officer doing an unannounced out-of-competition test.

**Story:** The officer met Kiprop at the gate after his 40 km run and had to watch him pass urine directly, even in the toilet. Kiprop's first sample was quick, but it was too diluted from all the water he had gulped to meet the specific-gravity requirement, so the officer stayed four hours, told him to stop drinking, and collected samples until the third was concentrated enough, then sealed and shipped all three to the lab as the rules require.
rounds.judge:
A

Both stories give the same doping-control explanation, but A explicitly covers more of the riddle's details (the gate, the toilet, the quick first sample, the four-hour wait, and shipping all three), while B never addresses the timing.
rounds.fact:
REAL
WADA's International Standard for Testing and Investigations requires continuous observation of the athlete after notification, direct witnessing of urine passage, and a minimum specific gravity of 1.005 (by refractometer) for a suitable sample. If a sample is too dilute, the officer must continue collecting, advise the athlete not to hydrate excessively, and send all samples to the lab (the lab also analyzes them), which matches the description.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
It explains the continuous observation, the advice to stop drinking, and why the officer sent all three samples to the lab even though only the third met the specific-gravity requirement.

rounds.riddle: When his night crew walked out on strike, the Montmartre bread shop still opened every single morning. Before dawn on the first day, the owner climbed a ladder and taped over one word of his own sign. A striker saw it and laughed: "He's announced our strike better than our banner." Customers queued and paid the same price, and the inspectors who came found nothing to fine.
rounds.chars: Gérard Vasseur (bakery owner and master baker); Lucie Marchand, his striking night-shift dough worker
rounds.story: With Lucie and the rest of the night crew on strike, nobody was left to knead and bake, so Gérard kept the Montmartre shop open by reselling frozen, factory-made baguettes that he only finished off in his oven. Under France's 1998 Loi Raffarin, a shop may call itself a "boulangerie" only if it kneads, shapes and bakes its bread on site and never freezes it, and using the title otherwise is consumer fraud, so he taped over the word "Boulangerie" on his sign, which kept the fraud inspectors from fining him but told the whole street that his own bakers had walked out.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Monsieur Garnier, owner of a Montmartre "Boulangerie-Pâtisserie."
**Character 2:** Luc, his night baker (on strike).

**Story:** French law lets a shop call itself a "boulangerie" only if its bread is kneaded and baked on site, so when Luc's crew walked out, Garnier bought his loaves from a baker across town and taped over "Boulangerie" before dawn, leaving only "Pâtisserie." Luc laughed that the covered word told every customer nobody was baking there, yet the same baguettes sold at the same price, and the fraud inspectors found no false claim to fine.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B's "Boulangerie-Pâtisserie" sign explains why covering just one word still left a working sign, while buying real loaves elsewhere naturally keeps the same bread at the same price without any false claim to fine.
rounds.fact:
REAL
France's 1998 law (often tied to Loi Raffarin, actually the 1998 decree/Law on the "boulanger" title, codified in Code de la consommation/Code rural) reserves the "boulangerie" name for shops that knead, shape and bake on site, with no freezing at any stage, and misuse is punishable as deceptive commercial practice.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
Buying bread from another bakery explains how the shop kept selling baguettes at the same price, while leaving “Pâtisserie” visible made the missing “Boulangerie” both a public sign of the strike and a legally accurate change.

rounds.riddle: At the Glen distillery on Islay, the new spirit was run off on a Friday and the cask was marked 11 gallons short on Monday. The only man who had touched it was honoured with a dram, and then fined. A woman who had never entered the warehouse told the owner to leave the missing gallons off the books and just pay the duty on the cask's full contents. The cask was found sealed, unbroken and dry-looking, and nobody was ever punished for the loss.
rounds.chars: Mairi MacLeod, the distillery owner; Alasdair Reid (excise officer)
rounds.story: The cask was filled under bond and the excise officer Alasdair Reid, the only man to touch it, tasted a dram from it, which was why he was fined. Mairi MacLeod's duty-paid declaration was legally safe because under the UK bonded-warehouse rules, duty is charged on the volume of alcohol filled into the cask, and the quantity lost to the "angel's share" evaporation is not deducted unless the cask is formally re-gauged and the spirit is lost under approved conditions. So the gallons gone missing were explained by ordinary evaporation through the oak, and her paying on the full fill was the cheapest way to avoid an inquiry into the cask's gauge.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Morag, the distillery owner's widowed mother, who grew up in a cooperage.
**Character 2:** Angus, the distillery's cooper.

**Story:** Angus built the new cask so tight that not a drop leaked, which earned him a dram, but he had used bone-dry, unseasoned oak, and over the weekend the thirsty staves soaked up 11 gallons of spirit while the outside still looked dry, so he was fined for wasting good wood. Morag knew from her cooperage days that the spirit was in the wood, not stolen, so she told her son to pay duty on the full fill and leave the "loss" off the books, which kept the exciseman from suspecting theft and meant nobody was ever charged.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A covers every odd detail: the dram rewards the tight cask, the fine punishes the unseasoned wood, and the spirit absorbed into the staves explains a sealed, dry-looking cask, while Morag's cooperage background explains her advice without her entering the warehouse. Story B leans on implausible weekend evaporation of 11 gallons, contradicts itself by making the dram the reason for the fine, and never explains why a woman who never entered the warehouse would know what to do.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
In UK bonded warehouses, duty is charged on the actual alcohol content at the time of removal, determined by gauging, and legitimate maturation losses (angel's share) are not dutiable, so the claim that duty is paid on the original fill volume without deduction is materially wrong.
rounds.alt_judge:
A
The cooper’s tight but absorbent cask explains the dry exterior, the dram, and the fine, while Morag’s cooperage experience explains how she recognized the apparent loss without entering the warehouse.

rounds.riddle:
At a Kerala wedding the lamp was lit and the garlands were exchanged, yet the groom's father stayed outside, forbidden to enter until the ceremony ended.
The bride's family fed everyone but kept one banana leaf unused at the head table.
At 11:40 the nadaswaram stopped mid-song, and the groom who had spent months abroad quietly signed a paper.
Nobody was upset, and the marriage was legal by noon.
rounds.chars: Groom, a Gulf-based nurse's fiancé named Anil; Sub-Registrar Mohan (government marriage registrar)
rounds.story: Anil, a Gulf-based engineer on a short leave, had arranged a temple wedding on a day when the registrar's office was closed, so his father, Mr. Nair, stayed outside because he was the legally required witness and had to be fetched from the registrar's office, where he was finishing the 30-day notice. Under the Kerala Registration of Marriages (Common) Rules, 2008, a marriage solemnized in a temple can be registered only by a joint application, and the registrar must verify the couple's presence and witnesses on the same day. Registrar Mohan therefore came to the hall, and the music was stopped at 11:40 because the rules also say a registration with a pending objection cannot proceed while a public ceremony is ongoing and disturbing the proceedings, so the quiet signing could be done at once and the marriage was legal by noon.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Arjun, the groom, a Gulf-based engineer.
**Character 2:** Raghavan, his father, a temple priest observing *pula* (ritual death-pollution) after his own mother died two weeks earlier.

**Story:** Because custom barred a mourning man from entering an auspicious ceremony, Raghavan watched from the gate, while the bride's family left a banana leaf empty at the head table to honour his late mother, who had blessed the match. When the muhurtham ended at 11:40 the nadaswaram stopped as planned, and Arjun signed the registrar's marriage certificate he needed for his spouse visa abroad, making the marriage legal by noon with everyone content.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B accounts for every odd detail: the father stays out because of mourning pollution, the empty leaf honours his late mother, the music stops at the scheduled end of the muhurtham, and the groom signs for a spouse visa, whereas Story A ignores the banana leaf and relies on invented, contradictory legal rules.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The Kerala Registration of Marriages (Common) Rules, 2008 exist, but they contain no provisions on the registrar attending a temple, a "same-day" presence verification, a rule that a pending objection blocks registration during a noisy public ceremony, or a witness being legally required to be fetched. The answer is also internally muddled, since a 30-day notice belongs to the Special Marriage Act, not to this procedure.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
It explains the father’s exclusion and the unused banana leaf through mourning and remembrance, while the ceremony’s scheduled end and the groom’s visa paperwork account for the timing and quiet signing.

rounds.riddle: Midnight, a West Texas rig, the drill still turning. A man in a clean hard hat shut off the lights on purpose and was thanked for it. The other man, covered in mud, threw his coffee away and walked off the site without a word. By morning, both were glad the rig had stood idle for eleven minutes.
rounds.chars: A young roughneck on his first week; the company man, an operator's wellsite supervisor (drilling engineer)
rounds.story: The new roughneck noticed the mud-logger's gas readings spiking and the pit level rising, which showed the well was taking a kick, so he hit the rig's emergency shutdown and killed the lights and engines before the company man arrived. The company man, who walked off in silence, knew that hydrogen sulfide from a sour-gas zone is heavier than air, smells like rotten eggs at first but then deadens the nose, and that his own contract and the Texas Railroad Commission's Rule 36 required the rig to shut in and have everyone move upwind to the muster point, so he threw down his coffee and left without speaking, as the procedure demands, to check the briefing area wind sock. The eleven-minute idle time was the lesser-known consequence: after the blowout preventer is closed, the crew must wait for the shut-in drill pipe and casing pressures to stabilize, which takes about that long, before anyone can read the true pressure needed to calculate the kill-mud weight, so the pause was the safe window for reading the gauges rather than wasted time.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Ray, the company safety man, whose hard hat was clean because he had just arrived on site.

**Character 2:** Dusty, the driller, coated in mud after the well "kicked" and blew drilling mud across the rig floor.

**Story:** When the gas alarm shrieked at midnight, Ray killed all electrical power and lights so no spark could ignite the gas cloud rising from the well. Dusty understood at once. He tossed his coffee (and the lit cigarette balanced on the cup), then walked silently upwind to the muster point without keying his radio, and by morning both were grateful that eleven dark, idle minutes had let the gas clear instead of blowing the rig sky-high.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B maps each detail cleanly: the clean-hatted safety man kills the lights to prevent a spark and is thanked, the mud-covered driller ditches his coffee and lit cigarette and walks silently upwind, and the eleven idle minutes let the gas clear. Story A muddles who did what, leaves the man in the hard hat and the thanks unexplained, and stretches to account for the eleven minutes.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The core pieces are real (kick indicators, H2S being heavier than air, Texas RRC Rule 36 for H2S, waiting for shut-in pressures to stabilize before calculating kill-mud weight), but they are combined wrongly. Killing the lights and engines is not a standard response to a kick, since shutting in means closing the BOP with power available, and an ESD of ignition sources is for gas release. A roughneck on his first week would not normally hit an emergency shutdown on his own, and the explanation of the company man's silence and the "eleven-minute" window is fabricated.
rounds.alt_judge:
B
It directly explains the clean hard hat, muddy clothes, discarded coffee, and silent exit, while making the blackout and eleven-minute pause part of the same emergency response.

rounds.riddle: Paris, the bakers' strike: every oven on the rue Oberkampf stayed cold for nine days. Yet at 4 a.m. on the sixth, one chimney smoked, and a man in a clean white coat left carrying warm loaves wrapped in a bedsheet. He paid nothing, and he was back before the first bus with exactly the flour he had taken in.
rounds.chars: Madame Lucette, a retired widow who owns the building's bakery lease; Étienne, a boulanger on strike (baker)
rounds.story: Étienne, a striking baker, could not bear to break the picket, but his late father's lease clause on the shop said the wood-fired deck oven must be fired at least once every seven days or the landlord could declare the premises abandoned and cancel the lease, so he secretly lit it on day six to protect Madame Lucette's tenancy.
